conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. I specialize in caring for moms in the weeks and months after birth, when so much is shifting all at once.

Today I’ll be using a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days, so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Anything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise, or unless safety is an immediate concern; then we’ll talk together about next steps. There are no right or wrong answers, and we’ll take it one gentle question at a time.

Let’s begin.  
Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

<med>EPDS-Q1</med>

[slow exhale]  
I… I can laugh sometimes, like if my husband does something goofy. But mostly it feels kind of far away, like I have to force it. Things that used to crack me up just feel kind of flat now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slight head-shake, voice quiet]  
Not very often… I mean, I laughed once when my best friend sent me a silly meme, but it felt like I had to remind myself how. Most of the time nothing feels that funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs a little, eyes on hands]  
Not really… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk by myself—but now it’s like I know I should look forward to them, yet I just… don’t. Even when I do go, I feel flat, like I’m watching someone else do it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[voice drops, eyes welling up]  
Yeah… a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I think it’s because I’m not soothing him right. Yesterday he wouldn’t nap, and I kept thinking, “Other moms know how to do this—why can’t I?” I tell myself it’s silly, but the guilt just keeps looping.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands in lap]  
Yes… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly picture him choking, or I’ll hear a siren and imagine something awful happened to my husband on his way to work. I know it’s unlikely, but I can’t stop the thoughts from barging in.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[shifts in chair, voice shaky]  
Sometimes... especially at night when the house is quiet. My heart will start racing and I feel like I can't breathe, but I don't know why. It's like this sudden wave of fear that something terrible is about to happen, even though everything seems fine.
Things have been getting on top of me

[quiet laugh, but not amused]  
Yeah… most days. Between feedings, laundry, trying to sleep when I can—some mornings I open my eyes and feel like I’m already drowning. I get through it, but it’s like I’m barely treading water, waiting for the next thing to go wrong.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[nods slowly, eyes tired]  
Yes... I lie down exhausted, but my mind just keeps spinning—did I burp him long enough, is he breathing, am I doing any of this right? I’ll finally drift off and then jerk awake sure I heard him cry. Some nights I’m awake for hours while everyone else sleeps.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, voice small]  
Yeah… most of the day, most days. It’s like there’s this heavy gray blanket over everything. I’ll look at the baby and feel love, but it’s mixed with this ache I can’t shake. I keep waiting for it to lift, but it just hangs there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[presses lips together, eyes glassy]  
A few times this week… yesterday I cried in the shower because I couldn’t get him to latch right, and the day before I just sat in the rocker with him asleep on my chest, tears dripping on his blanket. It hits out of nowhere sometimes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No—never. I feel low, but I would never want to leave him or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he deserves.

You've shared how the joy you once found in small pleasures now feels distant and how most days are clouded by a heavy, gray sadness. You described daily waves of worry, sudden panicky feelings at night, and a looping sense of guilt that you're not measuring up as a mom. Between feedings, laundry, and trying to rest, you feel as though you're barely keeping your head above water, and tears arrive without warning. Still, you clearly love your baby and want to feel better so you can care for him the way you hope to.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, forced laughter and states "nothing feels that funny anymore," aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment and emotional flatness, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses frequent, intense self-blame ('a lot,' looping guilt) tied to routine infant care, matching 'Yes, most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily intrusive worries (baby choking, husband harmed) that she cannot stop, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes episodic panic-like symptoms (heart racing, breathlessness, sudden fear) that occur 'sometimes,' aligning with 'Yes, sometimes</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," "already drowning," and "barely treading water," matching the highest distress level.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, repeated awakenings, and prolonged insomnia directly linked to unhappiness and anxiety, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness 'most of the day, most days' with persistent heaviness and ache, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple discrete crying episodes this week, triggered by breastfeeding struggles and sudden emotional surges, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 24/30 places you well above the 14-point cutoff indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med> and warrants urgent follow-up. You endorse <sym>depressed mood</sym> and <sym>loss of interest</sym> most of the day, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, <sym>diminished concentration</sym> (rumination), and <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> nearly every day, meeting <med>DSM-5 symptom count</med> criteria. High <sym>anxiety</sym> items suggest comorbid <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. Because you deny self-harm, immediate safety risk is lower, but severity requires rapid intervention. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or <med>psychiatrist</med> for evaluation and possible medication
3. Engage local <med>postpartum support group</med> or therapist trained in CBT or IPT
4. Enlist partner/family to handle one nightly feeding so you can obtain a 4-5-hour stretch of sleep
5. Practice 5-minute <med>breathing or grounding exercises</mad> when panic sensations start; keep lights low and use slow exhalation
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient-reported symptoms:
- Persistent low mood, sadness “most of the day, most days”
- Marked anhedonia—minimal enjoyment or anticipation of previously pleasurable activities
- Daily, excessive self-blame and guilt regarding infant care
- Recurrent, intrusive anxious thoughts and mental “looping”; spontaneous panic symptoms (palpitations, dyspnea) without clear trigger
- Frequent tearfulness and crying episodes
- Sleep disturbance driven by ruminating worries about infant safety
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and “drowning” in daily tasks

Observed signs:
- Flat affect, quiet voice, psychomotor slowing
- Teary when discussing guilt; hand-wringing, shifting posture during anxiety items

Pattern consistency:
Answers indicate congruent depressive and anxiety features present “most days” for at least the past week.

Safety screen:
Denies any self-harm ideation (Q10). No suicidal or infanticidal thoughts endorsed.

Screening significance:
High endorsement of items consistent with probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety. Meets clinical threshold for immediate follow-up assessment (PHQ-9 ≥ 10 equivalent) and consideration of formal diagnostic evaluation, supportive counseling, and possible medication management.

Next steps documented:
Provide scoring sheet, discuss findings, offer referral to obstetric mental-health team / outpatient psychiatric services; safety plan reviewed; crisis resources provided.
